Title: RUBAS: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning for Agent Safety
Abstract: The evolution of LLMs into tool-enabled agents creates a new class of safety challenges associated with real-world execution rather than simple text generation. Existing alignment methods often rely on coarse refusal signals or static supervision, making it difficult to balance safety with useful tool execution across diverse agentic risks. We introduce RUBAS, a rubricbased reinforcement learning framework for agent safety. RUBAS decomposes agent behavior into four dimensions: tool-use safety, argument safety, response safety, and helpfulness. These structured rubrics provide finegrained and interpretable rewards over complete agent trajectories, enabling reinforcement learning to optimize safe tool use while preserving task completion. Extensive experiments across multiple agent safety benchmarks and models show that RUBAS improves safety over standard alignment baselines, reduces tool-grounded hallucinations, and maintains competitive utility. Our results suggest that multidimensional rubric rewards provide an effective training signal for aligning LLM agents in safety-critical tool-use settings.
Major_Contribution_Result: RUBAS is a rubric-based reinforcement learning framework for tool-enabled agent safety that scores trajectories on tool-use safety, argument safety, response safety, and helpfulness. Across multiple agent safety benchmarks and models, the authors report improved safety over standard alignment baselines while preserving utility. On Qwen3-8B, average risk score falls from 52.7% to 15.9% with utility 79.5%; on GLM-4.7-Flash, average risk improves from 37.1% to 28.2% with utility 71.0%. Ablations indicate both multi-dimensional rubrics and online RL matter for alignment quality.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors state RUBAS is trained mainly on synthetic agent-safety scenarios that may not fully reflect deployed agents with ambiguous intents and side effects. Rubric quality depends on strong LLMs used to synthesize tasks/criteria. Experiments focus on thinking-mode models; non-thinking settings are not yet examined. RUBAS is not a complete safety solution and may fail on novel adversarial cases outside the training taxonomy; deployment should combine it with runtime monitoring, human confirmation, and red-teaming.
Critics: This is a training-time mitigation/alignment paper for tool-using agents, evaluated with aggregate risk/utility metrics rather than a universal ASR protocol across all agent threats. Results are model- and benchmark-specific (e.g., larger gains on Qwen than GLM in the reported averages). It contributes fine-grained trajectory supervision for agent safety evaluation, but does not cover MCP census threats, multimodal mobile agents, or post-mitigation continuous assurance alone.
